opus-5.5.text:
Conventional search engines were built for a human on the other end. You type a few keywords, you get ten blue links, and then you do the real work: you click, skim, decide what's trustworthy, go back, refine the query. The whole system is optimized around human attention, around getting you to click and, frankly, around ads.

An AI agent is a completely different kind of user. It doesn't need ten links ranked for clickability. It needs the right information, in a form it can actually reason over, packed efficiently into a context window. So when we started Parallel, the question was: what would the web look like if it were designed for AIs as the primary customer, not humans?

That changes a lot. Agents can express much richer intent than a few keywords. They can say, "I'm trying to figure out X, here's what I already know, here's what would count as a good source." We can take that full objective and return the most relevant passages, the tokens that matter, rather than a page the model has to wade through. That improves accuracy and cuts cost and latency, because you're not stuffing the context with junk.

The other big piece is that agents do deep, multi-step work. A human might run one search. An agent doing real research might need to run hundreds of queries, cross-reference sources, and verify claims. So we think about things like verifiability, citations, and calibrated confidence as first-class features. If an agent is going to act on what it finds, it needs to know how much to trust it.

So the value isn't "a slightly better search engine." It's infrastructure for a world where most web usage is going to be done by agents on behalf of people. The open web needs a new interface for that, and we think it should be one that's accurate, transparent about where information comes from, and fair to the people who create the content in the first place.

fable-5.1.text:
Parag: I think the starting point is that search engines were built for humans, and humans and agents want very different things from search. A person types a couple of words, scans ten blue links, clicks one or two, and does the synthesis in their own head. The whole product is optimized around that: a small number of results, ranked for click-through, delivered in a few hundred milliseconds because a human is waiting. An agent doesn't work that way at all. An agent has a task, not a query. It might decompose that task into dozens or hundreds of questions, it cares about the actual content of the pages and not the snippet, it wants evidence it can cite, and it's often perfectly happy to wait longer if that means getting the right answer instead of the fast one.

So when people bolt a conventional search API onto an agent, they're essentially forcing the model to pretend to be a human user. It writes a short query, gets back titles and snippets, then has to go fetch pages, parse them, figure out which ones are trustworthy, and iterate. Most of the tokens and most of the latency end up spent on that plumbing rather than on reasoning. And the quality ceiling is set by a ranking function that was never trained for what the model actually needs.

What we're trying to do with Parallel is build search where the model is the customer from the ground up. That changes a lot of decisions. You can accept a much richer input, a natural language description of the objective rather than keywords. You can return the relevant passages directly instead of making the agent go click. You can run many retrievals at once and let the system do the work of reconciling them. And critically, you can expose a dial on how much compute to spend, so a quick lookup is cheap and fast but a hard research question can run deeper and come back with something closer to a verified answer with sources.

The way I'd frame the value is in terms of the task, not the query. If you measure a search engine on whether the right link was in the top ten, the legacy engines look fine. If you measure it on whether an agent completed its job correctly, with the right facts and the right citations, at a reasonable cost, the gap gets large quickly. That's the metric we care about, because that's what the people building agents actually care about.

And I think this is going to matter more over time, not less. As agents get more capable, the bottleneck shifts from the model's reasoning to the quality of what it can see about the world. The web is still the richest source of information we have, and the interface to it for machines is honestly pretty bad today. Fixing that interface feels like one of the highest leverage things you can do for the whole ecosystem.

r002.rationale: It weighs answer quality and correctness against cost and speed, and describes adjusting compute so quick searches are cheap and fast while harder research goes deeper.

r003.rationale: It describes returning relevant passages and trustworthy evidence, but does not explain that reducing noise while preserving signal expands what the model can accomplish.

r004.rationale: It discusses parallel retrieval and a compute dial for search, but does not frame compute allocation across the model, agent, and search layers as the central approach.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is who the search is serving. A conventional search engine is designed for a person: you type a query, get a set of links, and then do the work of reading, comparing, and deciding what matters. An AI agent needs to do that entire loop itself.

So the value of Parallel Search is in how well it supports that task. Can the agent find the relevant information, get enough context to interpret it, and trace it back to a source? And can it do that with fewer calls and less unnecessary information in its context?

The way I’d evaluate it is by looking at the task the agent ultimately completes. Does it produce a better-supported answer? Does it finish faster and at lower cost? Returning useful search results matters, but helping the agent reliably finish the job is the real measure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is who you’re building for. A conventional search engine is designed around a human who types a query, looks at a page of results, clicks a few links, and figures out what matters. An agent needs to do that work programmatically, often as one step in a much larger task.

So the value isn’t just finding relevant links. It’s getting the agent useful information in a form it can reason over, with enough context and provenance to support its answer. And you have to think about the whole task: how many searches does it take, how much irrelevant material does the model have to process, and how reliably can it reach a useful result?

That’s how I’d frame the opportunity for Parallel Search: build the search experience around the agent’s needs, and measure success by whether it helps the agent complete the user’s task.

r002.rationale: It discusses useful information, search count, and reliable results, but does not frame the task as optimizing across quality, cost, and latency.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts useful information with irrelevant material, but does not explain that reducing noise while preserving signal increases what a model can accomplish.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe intelligent compute allocation across the model, agent, and search layers as a way to improve agent performance.
